articleSummary:

- Eight major Indian Railway stations, including Coimbatore (Kovai), are serving drinking water contaminated with human fecal Escherichia coli (E. coli), according to a shocking Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) report. The audit identifies the presence of dangerous E. coli in passenger water supplies and flags serious violations of drinking-water quality regulations across the network. The report points to gaps in water treatment, sanitation, and monitoring, raising public health concerns for travelers. No infection counts or laboratory-confirmed outbreak details are provided in the article. The findings prompt calls for immediate corrective action and stricter enforcement of water-safety standards for railways to prevent potential illness among passengers.
- Eight stations across four zones tested positive for E. coli in drinking-water sourced from water coolers: Coimbatore, Palakkad Junction; Hyderabad; CSMT Mumbai, Bhiwandi Road, Kalyan, Lonavala; Madhupur. articleSummary: Visceral leishmaniasis in Brazil is addressed, clarifying that dogs do not transmit the disease directly to humans; transmission occurs via the sand fly infected with the protozoan Leishmania infantum. Dogs can be infected for months before showing signs, which include weight loss, reduced appetite, hair loss, non-healing wounds, eye changes, nail overgrowth, and enlarged lymph nodes; without veterinary care, organ systems may be affected. Humans are impacted, and the issue is a public health problem in Brazil, highlighted by the Agosto Verde-Claro prevention campaign. Prevention priorities span both animals and environments: continuous use of repellent collars, vaccination where indicated, insecticidal products, and proper environmental management to reduce sand fly habitats. Home practices include yard cleaning, debris removal, waste control, and screens for kennels. Early veterinary consultation and a One Health approach are essential to break the transmission cycle and reduce year-round risk.

articleHeadline: Leishmaniasis: what it is and how to protect yourself.
articleSummary: Leishmaniasis in Botucatu, Brazil, is transmitted to humans by the sand fly (mosquito-palha) after it bites an infected animal; the parasite Leishmania chagasi is acquired by the vector from dogs or other animals and then transmitted to people. Cutaneous leishmaniasis starts as a small skin lesion that slowly enlarges into an ulcer over weeks to months; persistent changes in the nose, mouth, or throat may signal mucosal involvement. The visceral form is more severe, with fever lasting more than two weeks, weight loss, profound fatigue, reduced appetite, and abdominal enlargement; severe cases can cause anemia, weakness, and immune compromise, increasing susceptibility to other infections. Prevention emphasizes environmental hygiene (removing leaves, organic material, and trash) to reduce sand fly breeding, plus repellents, screens on doors/windows, and protective clothing from dusk to dawn when the vector is active.

articleHeadline: With 18 confirmed deaths from Brazilian spotted fever in São Paulo, a specialist from UMC warns about early diagnosis and prevention.
articleSummary: Brazilian spotted fever has caused 18 deaths and 19 confirmed cases in the state of São Paulo through July 2026, with fatalities concentrated in Piracicaba, Americana, Sorocaba, Campinas, São José dos Campos, Santo André, and São Bernardo do Campo; Alto Tietê reports no cases this year, though risk remains in rural, trail, and woodland areas. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent severe illness. Transmitted by ticks infected with Rickettsia rickettsii, the disease can be carried indoors by dogs. Initial symptoms are nonspecific, with fever, body pains, headache and malaise; by day three a red rash and purplish lesions on hands and feet may develop, signaling vascular involvement. Mortality can reach 80% if antibiotics are delayed. Laboratory confirmation may take up to two weeks, so treatment should start promptly when fever follows forest exposure. Prevention includes long pants, boots, light-colored clothing, prompt body and clothing checks, avoiding tall grass, and tick prevention for dogs.

articleHeadline: Middlesex County Resident Tests Positive for Zika Virus, First NJ Case in Six Years
articleSummary: Middlesex County resident diagnosed with travel-associated Zika virus; first New Jersey case since 2020, per the NJ Department of Health. Infection acquired abroad; destination and town undisclosed. Local risk remains extremely low; no continental U.S. transmission since 2018. Six travel-associated Zika diagnoses have been reported nationwide this year (CDC). Zika spreads primarily via Aedes aegypti bites, active after sunrise and around sunset; sexual and mother-to-fetus transmission are possible. Most infections are asymptomatic; about 20% develop fever, rash, red eyes, and joint or muscle pain lasting 2–7 days. Pregnancy poses higher risk; about 1 in 20 symptomatic pregnancies lead to congenital Zika syndrome (birth defects such as abnormal brain development, reduced head size, hearing loss, seizures). No vaccine or specific treatment; prevention focuses on mosquito bite avoidance and EPA-registered repellents. Updated data are available on the Vector-Borne Disease Data Dashboard; the 2015–2016 Brazil outbreak was the peak, with over 30,000 locally acquired U.S. cases, mostly in Puerto Rico.

articleHeadline: Doctors warn that influenza is far more severe in the elderly than in younger people, and urge stronger protective measures.
articleSummary: Influenza remains a seasonal threat in Thailand, with over 1 million cases nationwide in the Thai year 2568 and more than 200,000 infections and 25 deaths in the first half of 2026. Elderly individuals aged 60+ with chronic diseases face the highest risk of severe illness and complications such as pneumonia, heart attack, and extended hospitalization. Vaccination is emphasized as a key prevention, with a fourfold higher-dose influenza vaccine designed for older adults showing greater protection than standard-dose: infection reduction by about 24.22%, influenza-related hospitalizations reduced by 31.93%, and smaller reductions in cardiovascular-related admissions (6.6%) and heart failure (21.3%) relative to standard-dose. Thailand Association of Infectious Diseases recommends considering high-dose vaccines for those aged 60+. In addition to vaccination, public health measures—mask-wearing, frequent handwashing, and avoiding crowded places—are advised, particularly before and during the rainy season.
